items.title: Amazon has a plan to index the world’s online shopping data
items.summary: Amazon is reportedly building a project called World Product Graph, which would gather data on almost every product sold anywhere in the world, including items Amazon does not stock. According to a Reuters exclusive, the aim is to keep shoppers on Amazon.com and give AI shopping agents a reason to start their searches there. Amazon disputes the report's figures on its own assistant, saying they are outdated.
items.articleBody:
Amazon is reportedly working on an internal project that would turn its website into the main reference point for product information across the internet. According to an exclusive Reuters report published on November 13, the initiative is called World Product Graph. Its aim is to collect and organise data on almost every item sold anywhere in the world, including products Amazon does not stock itself.

Reuters says it based its report on an internal Amazon planning document, known as a PR/FAQ, and on people familiar with the matter. The central idea is simple: if Amazon holds the most complete and accurate catalogue of product details, shoppers have less reason to leave Amazon.com to compare options, check specifications or read about alternatives on other sites.

Why Amazon wants this now

The timing reflects a shift in how people shop online. Search engines such as Google have long been the starting point for product research, and rivals such as Walmart have been growing their e-commerce businesses. A new threat has also appeared in the form of AI shopping agents, which are assistants that search, compare and sometimes buy on a person's behalf. Reports on the plan name Meta's Muse and Perplexity among the tools Amazon is watching.

An agent that works for the shopper has no loyalty to any single store. Reuters reports that the people it spoke to see the product graph as a way to give those agents a reason to come to Amazon. If the best data on every product is on Amazon.com, an agent looking for answers is more likely to start there than at a competitor.

The problem with Amazon's own assistant

The report also says the document points to weaknesses in Amazon's own AI shopping tool. That tool launched as Rufus and, since May, has been marketed as "Alexa for Shopping." According to the report, the planning document acknowledged that the assistant sometimes gave inaccurate information, and a broader, cleaner product database was seen as a way to fix that.

Amazon disputes the picture. In a statement to Reuters, the company said the usage figures in the document are "significantly outdated." It also said its own data shows Alexa for Shopping is roughly 97% accurate worldwide.

Not the first attempt

The idea builds on earlier work. In 2025 it was reported that Amazon was developing a project called Starfish, which aimed to simplify how third-party sellers create product listings and to improve the quality of its catalogue data. World Product Graph appears to take that ambition much further. It would cover the whole market rather than only items listed on Amazon.

What is still unknown

Much remains unclear. The reporting rests on an internal planning document, and plans of this kind can change or be dropped before launch. It is not known when, or whether, World Product Graph will go live, and nothing is confirmed about how the data would be collected from other retailers. Nor is it clear how sellers, competing stores and regulators would respond to a company holding data on products it does not sell.

Why it matters

If the plan succeeds, it could strengthen Amazon's position as the default place to research and buy products, and it could pull traffic away from search engines and rival retailers. For shoppers, it could mean more consistent and detailed product information in one place. It would also add to the data and influence of a company that already dominates online retail. Competitors, sellers and AI developers will be watching closely to see whether Amazon moves ahead with it.
items.author: Kamali

items.title: Securing the agentic enterprise with data lineage
items.summary: As companies let AI agents pull data from many systems at once, security teams are finding that guarding apps, networks and devices is not enough. A sponsored MIT Technology Review report, produced with security firm Cyberhaven, argues that organisations also need data lineage: a record of where data came from, how it changed and where it went.
items.articleBody:
As businesses hand more everyday work to AI agents, a basic security question is getting harder to answer: where did the data in an agent's output actually come from? A sponsored report published by MIT Technology Review on November 4, 2026, produced with the data security company Cyberhaven, argues that the answer depends on a concept called data lineage.

Consider a simple example. A sales representative asks an AI agent for a customer's pricing. To respond, the agent may draw on several places at once: a restricted pricing system, internal messages and old archived quotes. The answer can look perfectly reasonable, yet it may combine information that was never meant to be mixed or shared with that person. Nobody reviewing the result can easily tell which source contributed what.

Why traditional security falls short

Most security tools were built around specific things: applications, systems, networks or individual devices. The report's central argument is that this approach is no longer enough when software agents act on behalf of employees and move information between many of those places at machine speed. Securing agents at scale, it says, requires understanding how data moves, and not only where it sits.

What data lineage means

Data lineage is a record of a piece of data's life: where it originated, how it moved, how it was changed and where it ended up. For human workers, security teams have long relied on this kind of trail in some form. The report says teams now need it across human, agent-driven and mixed workflows so that governance, accountability and trust can be maintained.

Industry analysts who follow the topic describe a related problem, sometimes called an agentic data lineage gap. Security teams can often see that an agent took an action, but not where its data came from, how it was transformed or where it was sent next. Without that context, an alert is harder to investigate and a policy is harder to enforce.

The wider framework

Cyberhaven's own guidance groups agent security into three pillars: visibility into what agents are doing, identity for the agents themselves, and guardrails that limit their behaviour. It describes data lineage as the link that connects the three. It also argues that fixed, rules-based guardrails tend to be brittle when agent behaviour changes quickly.

A vendor with a product to sell

Readers should keep in mind that the report is sponsored content and that Cyberhaven sells products in this area. The company launched an AI-native data security platform called Flow on July 28, 2026, and added an Agentic Data Security module to it in early November. The argument that lineage is essential is also the argument for buying such a tool. That does not make it wrong, but it should be weighed alongside independent research and other vendors' approaches.

What is still unknown

The report makes a case, but it does not settle how much lineage tracking organisations actually need, how well it works across different tools and agents, or what it costs in complexity and privacy. It is also unclear how quickly companies will adopt such controls compared with how quickly they are deploying agents.

Why it matters

Agents are being given access to more company data, and in many organisations the controls have not kept pace. Any company that lets agents handle customer, financial or internal information will need to be able to show where that information came from and where it went. Data lineage is one of the leading proposals for doing that, and the debate over how to implement it is only beginning.
items.author: Kamali

items.title: Critical Rails Flaw Lets Attackers Write Server Files via Crafted ImageMagick Uploads
items.summary: Rails has patched a critical flaw in its Active Storage upload component that could let an unauthenticated attacker write files to a server by uploading a specially crafted file, if the app processes uploads with ImageMagick. Fixed versions 8.0.5.2 and 8.1.4.1 were released on November 4, and teams are urged to upgrade and review their image-processing settings.
items.articleBody:
The Ruby on Rails team has fixed a critical security flaw in Active Storage, the framework component that handles file uploads. According to the project's advisory, published on November 4, 2026, an unauthenticated attacker could write arbitrary files to a server by uploading a specially crafted file, provided the application processes uploads with ImageMagick. The Rails advisory is tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 and carries a severity score of 9.8 out of 10.

How the flaw works

ImageMagick decides how to read a file based on its contents rather than its file name. Some of its internal format handlers, known as coders, do more than decode a picture. They can follow instructions inside the file that touch other files on the server. Reports on the advisory say Active Storage did not restrict any of these coders, and its image analyzer runs as soon as a file is attached. That means a crafted upload does not need a preview or a resized version to be requested before it can cause harm.

Applications that use the Disk storage service face an additional risk. The advisory says the same path can also allow arbitrary files readable by the application to be read, which could expose secrets and credentials.

Who is affected

Security analysts summarising the advisory say an application is exposed when three conditions are met. It uses Active Storage with ImageMagick for image processing, it accepts uploads from untrusted users, and its ImageMagick security policy does not already block the affected coders. One report notes that the default policies packaged by Debian and Ubuntu do not block them.

The affected versions of the activestorage package are those older than 8.0.5.2 and the 8.1 line before 8.1.4.1. Applications on other branches should check the official advisory for guidance.

What to do

The Rails team released the fixes in versions 8.0.5.2 and 8.1.4.1 on November 4. Teams running affected applications should upgrade as soon as possible. Where an immediate upgrade is not possible, the advisory describes a workaround that involves tightening ImageMagick's security policy so the risky coders are blocked.

For apps that use the Disk service, the maintainers advise rotating secret_key_base and any other secrets the application process could read, since those may have been exposed if the flaw was abused. Security writers also recommend reviewing upload activity and looking for unexpected file changes on servers that met the conditions above.

A familiar pattern

The incident is another reminder that image-processing tools do more than open pictures. Coverage of the Rails flaw points to earlier problems involving ImageMagick in other products, including a WordPress issue and a Discourse image pipeline attack, where the tool was pushed into reading or acting on files it should not touch. The common lesson is that uploads from untrusted users need strict limits on what the software handling them is allowed to do.

What is still unknown

Reports differ on the identifier. Some outlets say no CVE number had been assigned when the advisory was published, while another cites CVE-2026-66066, so readers should check the official advisory for the current status. None of the coverage reviewed said the flaw was being exploited in the wild, and the vulnerability had not been listed in CISA's known-exploited catalogue at the time one analyst wrote about it. That could change.

Why it matters

Rails runs a large number of online stores, software-as-a-service products and startup apps, and many of them accept file uploads from the public. A flaw that needs no login and can lead to file writes and secret exposure is one that attackers tend to look at quickly. Any organisation running Rails with ImageMagick should confirm its version, apply the update and rotate secrets where the advisory calls for it.
items.author: Kamali

items.title: Xen Hypervisor Flaws Let One Malicious VM Read and Write Any Other VM's Memory
items.summary: The Xen Project has disclosed two flaws, tracked as XSA-523, that let a malicious virtual machine read and change the memory of other VMs on the same host, including the privileged control domain known as dom0. Patches are available, but there is no workaround, so operators of Xen-based servers need to update the hypervisor and restart the host.
items.articleBody:
Two serious flaws in the Xen hypervisor can let a malicious virtual machine break out of its isolation and read or change the memory of other virtual machines on the same physical server. The Xen Project disclosed the problems on November 3, 2026, in security advisory XSA-523, which covers two vulnerabilities tracked as CVE-2026-102703 and CVE-2026-102704. The advisory's impact statement says a malicious guest can read and write arbitrary memory belonging to other domains, including dom0.

What dom0 is and why it matters

Xen runs ordinary workloads in guest virtual machines, while a special privileged virtual machine called dom0 manages everything else on the host. By default, dom0 has full permissions. If a guest can write into dom0's memory, the separation between tenants on that server effectively disappears. Vates, the company behind XCP-ng, describes the risk as a single compromised guest being able to take over the whole host.

How the flaws work

Xen lets one virtual machine grant another access to specific pages of its memory, and the hypervisor checks permissions so that each VM only touches what it has been granted. According to coverage of the advisory, the flaws sit in the code that handles grant copy operations. To save time when copying a batch of data within the same memory page, Xen reuses permission checks it has already made. In some cases it failed to check again when it should have, which let a guest reach memory it had no right to access.

An attacker who exploits this could read other tenants' data, keys and secrets held in memory, and write into other domains. Security researchers who examined the issue say Xen versions from 4.6 onward are affected.

Who is affected

Multi-tenant servers, where several customers' virtual machines share one host, carry the highest risk. That includes cloud and hosting providers as well as organisations that run Xen-based platforms. Vendors built on Xen, including XCP-ng, Citrix XenServer and Qubes OS, have published their own update guidance. Qubes, for example, has a fixed Xen package for Qubes 4.3 that is rolling out in stages and requires a restart of dom0 afterwards.

What to do

The advisory reports no known workaround, so the only real fix is a patched hypervisor from the Xen Project or from the platform vendor. A new hypervisor only takes effect after the host is restarted, so operators need to plan maintenance windows. Anyone who builds Xen from source should read the instructions for their release carefully, because the patches may depend on other code changes that are missing from the downloaded files. At least one security analysis also notes that older Xen releases may have no upstream patch available, which leaves those deployments reliant on vendor support or an upgrade.

What is still unknown

No attacks using these flaws had been reported at the time of the coverage reviewed. It is also not yet clear how many older or self-managed deployments will be left unpatched, or how quickly hosting providers will complete the required restarts.

Why it matters

Hypervisor isolation is the foundation of virtualisation security. Customers who share hardware rely on it to keep their data separate, and a guest-to-host escape undermines that promise. The flaws are a reminder that even mature, widely reviewed software can hide serious mistakes in its most sensitive code. Organisations that run Xen directly, or buy hosting from providers that do, should check their patch status and ask whether affected hosts have been updated and restarted.
items.author: Kamali

items.title: Radio With No Radar: Why Agent Runtime Security Fails Without the Layers Beneath It
items.summary: Many AI agent security products promise to stop harmful actions in real time, but a security-vendor analysis argues that promise only holds when an agent's traffic passes through a gateway the company controls, which most agents never do. The piece says runtime enforcement needs a clear picture of what agents can reach and what is normal for them, or it is working blind.
items.articleBody:
Nearly every pitch for AI agent security now ends with the same promise: the product will stop the bad action in real time. A recent analysis published by The Hacker News on November 4, 2026, which appears to come from the security vendor Reco, argues that this promise is only true for a narrow kind of agent. It holds for agents whose traffic passes through a gateway the company owns. Most agents, the author says, never touch one.

Where agents actually run

The argument starts from a practical observation. Many of the agents employees use today live inside platforms and applications the company does not fully control, such as business software, assistants and tools built into services. In that setting the application itself is the runtime. A security team cannot simply place an inspection point in front of the agent, because the agent's activity never travels through a path the company owns.

The article illustrates the risk with an everyday case. An employee approves an action without realising the assistant is about to bypass the sanctioned system, and an unknown number of external recipients end up receiving email from a personal account instead of the approved channel. Nothing in that sequence looks dramatic, which is why it is hard to catch.

Radio without radar

The headline's metaphor sums up the thesis. The author compares runtime enforcement to an air-traffic controller who has a radio but no radar. The controller can issue commands with authority, but without knowing which plane is where and where it is headed, every instruction is a guess delivered confidently.

In this picture, runtime enforcement is the radio. The radar is what the article calls posture: what an agent is able to reach, what counts as normal behaviour for it and whom it is acting on behalf of. The article says runtime controls only work well when that underlying picture exists.

Why context decides whether controls work

Without context, security teams face a familiar trade-off. If a tool blocks too much, the business finds ways to route around it. If it blocks too little, it becomes little more than a logging system that adds delay. The article's conclusion is that useful runtime security must stop the genuinely harmful action without stalling the many legitimate actions around it, and that takes knowledge of identity, permissions and normal behaviour.

The argument rests on three points: agents run inside platforms, individual components of those platforms can themselves be targets, and good decisions need context. Together these suggest that runtime protection is the last step in a chain of controls rather than a replacement for the earlier ones.

Others make a similar point

Other security writers have reached related conclusions. Analysts who focus on non-human identities argue that runtime detection often sees behaviour only after an identity boundary has already been crossed, and that an agent holding a broad access token can do real damage before an alert arrives. Their advice is to start with identity and permission design and use detection to confirm the limits are holding.

A vendor's perspective

Readers should remember that this analysis comes from a company that sells products in the layers it says are neglected. The argument can be right and still serve a commercial purpose. It should be weighed against independent research and against the claims of runtime-security vendors, who would say that real-time enforcement is necessary even if it is not sufficient.

What is still unknown

The article is an opinion and framing piece and not a measurement. It does not establish how many enterprise agents operate outside company-owned gateways, how often runtime tools fail for lack of context, or how much the layered approach it recommends would cost or reduce risk in practice.

Why it matters

Companies are adopting agents faster than they are building the controls around them. A tool that promises to block bad actions in real time can create false confidence if the security team cannot see what the agent can access or what it normally does. The practical lesson is to check that agent security rests on visibility and permissions first, and to treat real-time blocking as one layer rather than the whole defence.
items.author: Kamali

items.title: China-Aligned Hackers Hijack Sogou Input Method DNS Requests to Deploy DarkVigil Backdoor
items.summary: Researchers at ESET say a China-aligned group called SlippyNunchucks hijacked internet lookups made by the Windows version of Sogou Input Method, a popular Chinese-language typing tool, to install a spying backdoor called DarkVigil. Tencent fixed the weakness in version 16.10, and users are urged to update.
items.articleBody:
A China-aligned hacking group has turned a popular Chinese-language typing program into a delivery route for spyware, according to research published by the security firm ESET on November 4, 2026. The group, which ESET calls SlippyNunchucks, abused the way the Windows version of Sogou Input Method fetched part of its settings, and used it to install a backdoor known as DarkVigil. Sogou Input Method is a widely used input method editor developed by Tencent.

How the attack worked

ESET says a component of Sogou Input Method requested a "brand-promotion" configuration from a Sogou server over plain, unencrypted HTTP. Because that traffic was not protected, the attackers could use DNS hijacking, a technique that quietly redirects a program's lookup to a different server, to send those requests to infrastructure they controlled. That server returned a malicious configuration instead of the real one.

The altered configuration then led a legitimate Sogou component to download files that included a signed program and a booby-trapped library of the same name that it loaded. This method, known as DLL side-loading, makes the malicious code run under the cover of a trusted program. The end result was the DarkVigil implant running on the victim's computer.

What DarkVigil is

DarkVigil, also known as FDMTP, is a modular toolset written in .NET with more than 20 plugins. ESET has tracked the malware and its operator since early 2025. The activity was described as part of a surveillance campaign, which points to espionage rather than ordinary financial crime.

Timeline and victims

ESET says the Sogou activity began on July 1, 2026, and that victims were spread across six countries. The activity followed an earlier supply-chain compromise involving the software QuickFox. The researchers saw the group switch to Sogou three days after QuickFox released a clean version. Other applications mentioned as having been abused by the same actor include QingTalk, MiYunChat, SoftCam and tawk.to.

The number and spread of victims first made the researchers suspect a software exploit, but the investigation traced the problem to the insecure connection instead.

The fix

Tencent addressed the issue in Sogou Input Method version 16.10, released on October 30, 2026. According to security summaries of the research, the update moves the affected requests from HTTP to HTTPS and adds certificate validation, which prevents a redirected server from impersonating the real one. Users should update to version 16.10 or later. Security teams are advised to watch for unexpected files named after Adobe software inside Sogou's components folder and for unusual network connections from the app. ESET's report contains the full technical indicators.

Not the first Sogou problem

This is not the first time Sogou Input Method has been used this way. In September 2026, Gen Digital reported that a separate, now-patched flaw in the software was exploited by another China-linked group to deliver a different backdoor.

What is still unknown

ESET has not established where the DNS hijacking took place. The researchers say possibilities include compromised routers with altered DNS settings, routers carrying a DNS-hijacking implant, or interception at the level of an internet provider. It is also unclear how many people were ultimately infected, who the specific targets were, and whether the group has other delivery routes ready.

Why it matters

The case shows how a harmless-looking background request, such as one for a small image or settings file, can become an attack path when it is not encrypted. Because the traffic looked like normal application behaviour, victims had little chance of noticing. Users and organisations with Sogou Input Method installed should update it, check their router and DNS settings, and treat any software that still uses plain HTTP for updates or configuration as a risk.

items.title: Apple Music's upcoming feature will let you record yourself doing karaoke
items.summary: Apple Music is adding a karaoke video feature called Selfie Sing, which lets iPhone users film themselves with the front camera while singing along to on-screen lyrics, then save or share the clip. The feature was spotted in the first iOS 27.3 developer beta, with a public release expected in December.
items.articleBody:
Apple Music is preparing a new karaoke-style feature called Selfie Sing that lets people record videos of themselves singing without leaving the app. The feature appeared in the first developer beta of iOS 27.3, which Apple released on November 3, 2026, and a public release is expected in December.

What Selfie Sing does

With Selfie Sing, an iPhone user can sing along to a song while the front-facing camera records them, with the lyrics shown on screen. According to the description shown in the feature, users can adjust the vocal effects on their voice, then save the video or share the performance with friends. Until now, anyone who wanted to make a singing video would typically have to switch to another app to film it.

The feature builds on Apple Music Sing, the karaoke mode that Apple introduced in late 2022 with iOS 16.2. That tool lets listeners reduce the original singer's vocals and follow animated lyrics. Selfie Sing adds the camera on top of it.

Who found it and how to try it

The feature was first spotted by Aaron Perris in iOS 27.3 beta 1. Beta users can find it by searching Apple Music for a playlist named Selfie Sing. Tech sites report that the playlist is visible even on iPhones running iOS 27.2, but the option to turn on the camera and record only appears on the iOS 27.3 beta.

Early limits

The feature is clearly still in testing. Coverage of early hands-on use says only a small number of songs support it so far, with one report counting six. It also appears to be limited to iPhones. AppleInsider reported that the camera option did not show up on an iPad Pro running the iPadOS 27.3 beta. Aaron Perris's demonstration video used an Animoji in place of his face, but reports say Selfie Sing does not support Animoji yet.

Other changes in the beta

Selfie Sing is not the only Apple Music change in this beta. 9to5Mac reports that iOS 27.3 also improves the lyrics view when the phone is held in landscape orientation.

What is still unknown

Beta features can change or be removed before release, so the final version of Selfie Sing may look different. It is not yet clear how many songs will be supported at launch, whether it will come to the iPad or other devices, what the sharing options will be, or whether it will be available in every region where Apple Music operates. Apple has not published detailed information about the feature in the coverage reviewed.

Why it matters

Short singing videos are a popular form of content on social platforms, and music services have been looking for ways to give listeners more to do than press play. By adding recording and sharing directly to Apple Music, Apple is making its app a place where people can create content as well as listen. If Selfie Sing launches broadly in December, it could also give Apple Music subscribers a reason to spend more time in the app and put it in competition with the karaoke and video features of other music and social apps.
items.author: Kamali

items.title: Binance attackers used fake job interviews to pull off $6.3 billion crypto heist
items.summary: Binance says the record $6.3 billion theft from the exchange began months earlier, when attackers used fake job interviews and tampered software to compromise the computers of its engineers. The FBI has reportedly blamed North Korea, while Binance's account shows how social engineering can open the door even at the world's largest crypto exchange.
items.articleBody:
Binance has shared more details about the cyberattack that cost it roughly $6.3 billion in digital assets, the largest crypto theft on record. The exchange said on November 3, 2026, that the attackers did not break in through a single technical flaw. Instead, they spent months preparing, using fake job interviews and tampered software to take over the computers of its own engineers.

How the attack began

According to Binance's account, as reported by several outlets, the attackers used a bogus job interview and malicious software hidden in an advertisement to compromise the computers of two software engineers. They then used a third engineer's computer to drain the funds. One report says the chain started in June, when a member of Binance's wallet developer team downloaded an AI tool that had been tampered with.

The details point to a patient operation. A fake recruitment process gives an attacker a believable reason to contact an engineer, ask them to run code or install software, and gain access to a device that may hold sensitive credentials. In this case the targets were developers who worked close to the systems that move customer funds.

Who is blamed

Engadget reports that the FBI says North Korea was behind the attack. Axios similarly reports that North Korea appears to have used a fake job interview as part of its months-long preparations. Another outlet links the activity to a North Korean group known as TraderTraitor, a name previously associated with attacks on crypto companies that used fake job offers. Binance's own statement, as summarised in these reports, focused on the methods used rather than on naming a culprit, so the attribution should be treated as reported rather than as a final finding.

How long it lasted

One report says the thieves were still moving crypto out of the exchange nearly four hours after the first theft. That detail suggests the attackers had access that could not be shut off immediately, although the full timeline of Binance's response has not been set out in the coverage reviewed.

Who is affected

Binance has not been described in these reports as passing the losses on to customers in the coverage reviewed here, and it is important to check the exchange's own updates on this point. The incident is nonetheless a serious event for the whole crypto industry, because Binance is the world's largest exchange and the theft is far larger than previous record heists.

Why the method matters

The case is a warning that the weakest point in a company's security is often a person's workstation rather than the exchange's core systems. Even a firm with advanced defences can be breached if an employee runs a malicious file during what looks like a job application. It also shows how attackers are turning to trusted tools, including AI tools, and to advertisements as ways to distribute malware.

Security experts commonly advise companies to keep developer machines separate from systems that can move funds, to require approval from more than one person for large transfers, and to train staff to treat unsolicited job offers and tests with caution. Individuals applying for jobs should be wary of any recruiter who asks them to download software or run code on a work device.

What is still unknown

Many questions remain. Binance has not publicly detailed how much of the stolen crypto can be recovered or frozen, and law enforcement has not said how the funds were laundered. It is also unclear exactly how the attackers moved from three compromised computers to the systems that held the assets, and whether other firms were targeted using the same approach.

Why it matters

A theft of this size shakes confidence in the safety of crypto exchanges and is likely to bring more scrutiny from regulators and law enforcement. It also reinforces the concern that state-backed hackers are using crypto theft to raise money. For companies of every size, the lesson is that a convincing recruiter message can be as dangerous as a software vulnerability.
